articles.title: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
articles.content: Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach... And look, the Boss has his office door open! C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D ! ... The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open. His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us. And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas. "AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop. He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town. ... "For the security system," the Boss teases. I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same. The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea. >clickety< >tap< "Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed." >tappity< "And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too." "It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to. "A virus?!" the Boss gasps. "I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing. ... So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him. Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow... >tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety< On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously. >tappity< >tap< The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight. On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling. >bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip< >ring< "Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback. "It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!" Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard. "What do I do?" the Boss gasps. "It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!" "I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks. DAMMIT! >tappity< >click< >tap< >tap< Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device... The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan. ...two hours later... "So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden. "Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor." "It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation." "It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used." "Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask. "No, more like lighter fluid." "Oh," I say,…
articles.author: Simon Travaglia

articles.title: Garmin Enduro 4 review: monster MIP battery life makes this a value alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro
articles.content: Memory-in-pixel displays are becoming rarer on the best Garmin watches , but those who prefer them are still well served by the Enduro line. If battery life is your primary concern, the Enduro 4 delivers in spades. It lasted me 16+ days on a charge, around 50% longer than even the best sports watches with AMOLED displays for battery life, like the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro or Suunto Vertical 2. Garmin hasn’t held back on features either, with the Enduro 4 getting most of the same key sports tracking tools as the Fenix 9 Pro, in a lighter case and at a lower price. It’s an attractive package, but the elephant in the room is that the Enduro 3 is also getting nearly all the same new features as the Enduro 4 through software updates, has a similar design and the same incredible battery life, and undercuts the new watch in sales. Garmin Enduro 4 review: Price and availability (Image credit: Future) The Garmin Enduro 4 launched in October 2026 and costs $899 in the U.S. and £799 in the U.K. It’s the same launch price in the U.S. as the Enduro 3, but the latter is now available for £699/$799. It’s a cheaper alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro Solar, which is the MIP option of the Fenix line-up and starts at $1,099. Garmin Enduro 4 review: Design and display (Image credit: Future) The Garmin Enduro 4 is a large but lightweight watch that uses Garmin’s familiar five-button setup. It has a 51mm case and is thick, but being mostly made from plastic means it’s significantly lighter than the 51mm watch in the Fenix 9 line-up. It has a titanium bezel and a sapphire crystal screen with solar panels to boost the impressive battery life even further in sunny conditions. The memory-in-pixel display is clear enough to read in all conditions, though I do think the Enduro 4 is less bright and readable than Garmin’s AMOLED watches when indoors or under tree cover. (Image credit: Future) There are some hardware changes and improvements from the Enduro 3. The Enduro 4 has a silver bezel with fewer yellow highlights, and under the hood it has more RAM, a faster processor for maps, and double the storage (64GB vs. 32GB on the Enduro 3). The new watch also comes with Garmin’s new ComfortFit band, which I like a lot more than the UltraFit band that ships with the Enduro 3, though you can also buy the ComfortFit band separately. (Image credit: Future) On the top of the watch is a built-in flashlight with four brightness levels and a red mode, and on its underside is Garmin’s Elevate Gen 5 heart rate sensor, which is the same sensor as the Fenix 9 series and Enduro 3. While it’s not a diveproof watch like the Fenix 9, the Enduro 4 has a 10 ATM rating and is waterproof. It also lacks the mic and speaker you do get on the Fenix. Despite its size, I found the Enduro 4 comfortable to wear 24/7 throughout testing. It’s not as attractive as the all-titanium Fenix 9 Pro, but the Enduro 4 is still a good-looking watch to wear outside your training. Garmin Enduro 4 review: Sports tracking and training analysis (Image credit: Future) Unless you’re desperate to go diving, the Enduro 4 has all the customizable sports modes you could ever need to track your workouts, including the improved rucking and rowing modes introduced on the Fenix 9. Runners, cyclists, swimmers and triathletes get the most detail in their sports modes, including an improved stamina feature that aims to provide guidance on how much energy you have left in endurance activities and how best to pace them. The Enduro 4 feeds all the data you track during workouts into an extensive suite of training analysis tools. It has all the top-of-the-range features you get on the Garmin Forerunner 970 and Fenix 9, including running economy estimates (when paired with the Garmin HRM 600 chest strap) and ratings for overall endurance and hill-running ability. Garmin offers greater depth of training analysis than any other brand I’ve tested, and while you might not want or need all this data, it’s there if you do,…

articles.title: Nvidia’s France Pledges Remain Intact: Varza
articles.content: Station F Director Roxanne Varza says French founders remain broadly reassured after Jensen Huang’s departure, with no sign Nvidia’s recent investment commitments are being withdrawn. She says the immediate damage appears reputational rather than operational, while prompting founders to consider the risks of building a company too closely around one leader. Speaking to Tom Mackenzie on the latest episode of Bloomberg Tech: Europe, Varza also noted the upheaval could eventually create opportunities for Europe to develop more sovereign alternatives to Nvidia’s technology stack. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: After BP monitoring smartwatches, HUAWEI reveals its first continuous glucose monitor
articles.content: Credit: Weibo / Huawei TL;DR HUAWEI has revealed a continuous glucose monitor in China. HUAWEI Sence G1 is the company’s first-ever Class III medical device. HUAWEI hasn’t shared details about availability but said it has been in development for over three years. HUAWEI may have been nearly wiped out of international markets by sanctions imposed on it during the first tenure of US President Donald Trump, but it remains at the top of China’s leaderboard. Along with its innovations across slab phones, foldables , and laptops —including laptops with foldable screens —HUAWEI also offers a broad range of wearables, including ones that monitor blood pressure . So far, the lineup has only comprised smartwatches and fitness bands, but HUAWEI is now adding a health-centric utility in the form of a glucose monitor. The HUAWEI Sence G1 is the company’s first continuous glucose monitor (CGM). The device works alongside other HUAWEI products, allowing users to view glucose levels on their phones, a smartwatch, or a HUAWEI fitness band. Besides monitoring a user’s glucose levels, the CGM will also alert them in case of any unusual spikes or dips.
articles.author: Tushar Mehta

articles.title: Is Mark Zuckerberg's cute new AI assistant a surveillance trap? Why child safety experts are sounding the alarm over Meta Muse
articles.content: Meta is already at the center of your online social life. Now, the company behind Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp wants a permanent spot on your desk. But Mark Zuckerberg’s latest products are triggering familiar red flags. Meta officially brands Muse AI as an 18+ productivity assistant. In reality, it looks more like a customizable toy. That cuddly, disarming design, paired with always-on microphones and ambient recording, is raising eyebrows. AI experts and children's digital safety campaigners speaking to TechRadar are warning that Muse AI and its upcoming Tamagotchi-style keychain companion, Muse Charm , create severe risks for children and teenagers. Following an initial rollout across the US and Canada in September, Meta’s new AI agent has begun to stretch its presence across Asia, landing in Japan , Singapore , and, soon, India . Now, despite the tech giant having yet to confirm a release date, reports suggest the company is eyeing Europe, with The Times revealing on Monday that the UK is first in line. As Muse edges closer to a global launch, is Meta’s new gadget setting the stage for the next youth privacy disaster? And are we ready to cope with the aftermath? Meta Muse: the cuteness trap (Image credit: Jacob Krol/Future) Already counting over 1.8 million daily users across the US and Canada, Muse is an AI agent that can carry out tasks on behalf of its users, like shopping online, booking vacations, or buying groceries. Muse Charm brings the AI agent into physical reality. The two-inch wearable hardware device reportedly has an OLED touchscreen, front and rear cameras, microphones, speakers, 5G connectivity, and USB-C charging, allowing users to talk to their Muse without needing to open their smartphone. At the visual center of the device is Jolly, a pink-cheeked, Labubu-style animated avatar that users can fully personalize — from its name, appearance, and outfits to its voice — transforming invisible software into a persistent, physical companion. While Mark Zuckerberg frames Jolly as a “fun, completely customizable character,” child safety advocates and behavioral researchers warn that this aesthetic functions as a psychological Trojan horse. Speaking to Fast Company , cuteness researcher Joshua Paul Dale notes that cute and child-like designs stimulate pleasure centers before users can evaluate risks, creating an instinctive urge to keep the device close. Moving beyond screen-based interactions, a wearable charm could then tap into innate social emotions, making conversations with ambient software feel as spontaneous and natural as speaking to a person standing beside you. That’s the warning coming from children's digital safety experts at the Canadian group The White Hatter , who note that such an always-on AI friend could fundamentally alter human attachment to the machine. Put simply, critics say that by leveraging nostalgia for Tamagotchis and popular designer toys, Meta is making a product capable of invasive surveillance feel harmless. Is the 18+ restriction a myth? AI safety specialist Kavya Pearlman — a former risk advisor during Meta’s Cambridge Analytica scandal — describes the toy-like aesthetic as a "deliberate attempt" to attract younger demographics. “This company has a lot of information that it knows will work towards gaining access to certain age groups,” she said. Meta, however, has so far rejected claims that Muse is directly targeting children. "This is a story in search of a story,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED . Roberts insists the avatar customization simply brings users joy, while pointing out that the company requires everyone using the Muse app to provide their date of birth. When approached by TechRadar, a Meta spokesperson also explained that age checks will include analyzing links between users’ Muse accounts and their Facebook or Instagram accounts. In the absence of a clear signal that they’re over 18, a credit card verification will be required to keep using the…

articles.title: UK firms are spending billions on hidden infrastructure costs — money they can't spend on hiring or AI
articles.content: UK enterprises are overspending on infrastructure, and AI is making this more unpredictable AI platform and model licensing fees are more of an issue than token-based pricing models Companies are having to cut back on hiring and training as a result New research has revealed UK businesses are losing £3.8 billion every year to unexpected infrastructure costs – a figure that rises to £47.4 billion across the UK, US, Japan, Italy, Germany, France, Australian and New Zealand. And that's not the amount that businesses are spending on infrastructure – it's only the portion of cash being spend that they weren't expecting to spend, the study from Wasabi and the Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) found. Around one-third (32%) of the overspending in the UK is attributed to AI and ML infrastructure, the research found, with one in five (22%) UK businesses describing this are of spending as 'unpredictable'. Unexpected infrastructure spend is eye-watering, and AI is making it unpredictable By far the highest infrastructure overspend category was AI platform and model licensing fees (66%), far ahed of token and usage-based charges (36%) even though the apparent ongoing shift from seat-based to consumption-based models has been criticized for making spend more unpredictable. The scale of overspend is also particularly alarming, because nearly three-quarters (73%) of businesses globally reported either a moderate or significant budget pressure. Three in four (77%) British companies have also had to make at least one cost-driven trade-off during the previous 12 months, including cutting new hires across tech roles (38%), limiting their tech investments (37%) or spending less on worker training schemes (34%). "This means hiring and investment in new technologies are postponed or reduced as budgets are redirected to cover unexpected charges," CEBR head of economics advisory Owen Good summarized. "[Businesses] are blindsided by unpredictable infrastructure costs that prevent them from driving their innovation agendas forward," Wasabi COO Marty Falaro added. CEBR modelling quantified these impacts, noting that recovered money otherwise overspent on infrastructure could actually be redirected to support over 8,200 jobs.
articles.author: Craig Hale

articles.title: I tested the DJI Osmo 360 II and Insta360 needs to be seriously scared
articles.content: “Uh oh,” is what Insta360 will doubtless have thought when the DJI Osmo 360 II launched. And it should’ve been worried. Up to now, Insta360 has been the undisputed king of 360 tech. But that reign has come to an end. It all comes down to one thing: 8K/60fps, which the DJI Osmo 360 II can shoot. The flagship Insta360 X6, meanwhile, cannot, topping out at 8K/50fps. Insta360 is simply not there yet with the tech, and in fairness, that’s understandable. 8K at 60fps in 360 degrees puts extreme demands on a pocket-sized camera, its processor, memory, battery and thermals. But somehow DJI has achieved it – which means it’s now ahead in the race. Even if the Osmo 360 II isn’t the best 360 camera in every area, it does the most important thing right now. It gives content creators the flexibility of 4K reframing from 360 footage at a frame rate fast enough for high-octane footage, and usable enough for YouTube. So should you buy this camera? Find out in my full DJI Osmo 360 II review. DJI Osmo 360 II review: Specs Starting price $699 / £509 Max video resolution 8K/60fps (360); 4K/120fps (Single lens) Sensors 2x 1/1.1-inch Stabilization Yes Screen 2-inch LED Internal memory 105GB MicroSD slot Yes Pre-recording Yes Wireless mic hookup Yes, via Bluetooth Wired mic hookup Yes Connectivity Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB-C Water resistance 33ft (10m) Battery 2,150 mAh Size 2.4 x 1.4 x 3.2 inches Weight 6.4 ounces DJI Osmo 360 II review: Price & availability (Image credit: Future) Unsurprisingly, given this is a flagship 360 camera, the Osmo 360 II isn’t cheap, opening the register at a whopping $699 in the U.S. at Amazon for the standard bundle with basic accessories. If you want accessories, the Adventure Combo I tested, with extra batteries and a selfie stick, costs $829 . Of course, this is thanks to U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. It’s also worth noting that, resulting from its feud with the U.S. government, DJI has withdrawn first-party support in the States, meaning no care plans if the camera needs repair. In the U.K., the Osmo 360 II starts at £509 , which undercuts the Insta360 X6 by over £100. And U.K. consumers also get access to a wider range of accessories bundles at Amazon, so they can tailor their spend to exactly what they need. This pricing is comparable to the Insta360 X6, which also starts at $699. In my opinion, the 360 II is a much better buy thanks to the higher 60fps frame rate. In the U.K., where the 360 II is both more powerful and cheaper, it’s a total no-brainer. If you’re on a tighter budget, though, I’d advise checking out the Insta360 X5 ($549), GoPro MAX2 ($499) or the OG DJI Osmo 360 ($494). All shoot 8K 360 footage, just not at 60fps. DJI Osmo 360 II review: Design & controls (Image credit: Future) The Osmo 360 II is designed more or less the same as its predecessor. It looks the same, measures the same, and weighs the same. That means it’s a squat-looking thing, especially compared to the lankier X6. It isn’t small though, at 2.4 x 1.4 x 3.2 inches, nor is it light at 6.4 ounces, so if you’re after something more suited to mounting on a helmet, check out an action camera like the DJI Osmo Action 6 . Versus the OG Osmo 360, there have been no radical updates to the display, which still isn’t an OLED; no updates to the internal memory, which is still 105GB (although over double the X6’s 47GB); and no updates to waterproofing, which is rated at 33 feet (half the 66 feet of the X6). (Image credit: Future) The controls are essentially the same, with two buttons on the back for recording and mode changing, a power button, and most tweaks done via the menu system or app. I found the Osmo 360 II’s record button fiddly to press with gloves on. And while I like DJI’s menu, it’s a little busy-feeling on the small display — the X6’s bigger display makes it slightly easier to use in the heat of the moment. Overall though, no major complaints controls-wise. Mounting (Image credit: Future) The Osmo 360 II uses the same quick-release…

articles.title: Workers don't mind if AI is making their employer more productive  — so long as they get paid well
articles.content: UK workers are prepared to use AI so long as its benefits are also shared with them Employees worry they don't have enough time and resources to keep up with skills Companies should be more transparent in supporting their workers One in three UK workers would expect what insurance group Howden describes as an 'AI dividend' – a higher pay – if their employer were able to achieve significant productivity gains or cost savings through the use of AI. The study of over 2,000 employees found a general acceptance toward AI, so long as its benefits are also passed onto them and not just the company. Those impacted by AI would also expect shorter working hours (16%), greater job security (15%) and a bonus (13%) if their company managed to unlock AI's benefits. Workers want to benefit from AI as much as their employers Despite an appetite for AI's benefits to be passed onto them, half (49%) worry they could be expected to complete even more work because of the time savings and another half (50%) fear AI could soon be used to assess their performance. A separate study has already demonstrated how workers feel pressured to use AI, showing that they use it regardless of its benefits just to keep managers happy. But before all of this becomes a reality, many companies still need to roll out AI across workers' environments. One on two worry it could be introduced faster than they understand it and 53% are worried they won't have time to learn the new skills on top of their existing workloads. The report found that simply providing access to AI training isn't enough – workers need fully support, including dedicated learning time. "With the workforce being central to the AI-productivity journey, our research show’s there’s a misalignment in expectations that must be addressed to improve the chances of success," Howden Employee Benefits & Wellbeing MD Cheryl Brennan wrote. The UK Government has already set out plans to upskill 10 million workers in AI by 2030, but uptake has reportedly been low and Howden is reminding employers that they must also play a role in their duty to workers. Brennan concluded with the need for "dialogue and action regarding pay, progression and transparency," keeping human workers in the loop and granting them access to AI's benefits.

articles.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
articles.content: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk. The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it. The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see. "Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said. In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping. Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed. The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025. And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018. Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch. "I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said. With hundreds of reports already…

articles.title: 5 AI agents you can actually use on Android in 2026 (and who should use them)
articles.content: Credit: Megan Ellis / Android Authority The AI industry has evolved significantly over the last few years. While chatbots remain one of the most common entry points into the world of AI, agentic systems are also gaining momentum. Early on, most agents had pretty limited capabilities, but that’s slowly changing as agents emerge that not only assist you with minimal manual oversight, but also offer deeper control over apps, platforms, and even Android itself. Agentic AI could transform how we do many tasks, from planning and tracking finances to scheduling our lives and more. Right now, there are multiple different types of agentic AI systems out there. Let’s take a look at just five of the most interesting platforms out there, designed as semi-autonomous assistants useful to a wide range of folks, from everyday users to power users and professionals.

articles.title: How Shanghai fund manager Kang Wei introduced his wife Alice Huang to Jensen and built $7.5 billion Nvidia AI GPU smuggling operation
articles.content: Jensen Huang had a stunning fall from grace — from being one of the richest people on Earth and one of the primary drivers of the AI boom to being implicated in two extramarital affair scandals and resigning from Nvidia in under two weeks. While many are focused on the former Nvidia chief’s relationship with Alice Huang, who was allegedly passing on information to Chinese intelligence , the Wall Street Journal dug deeper into the person who introduced her to Jensen — Kang Wei, a star fund manager in Shanghai who also happened to be Ms. Huang’s husband. There have been reports that Kang Wei met Jensen Huang in the 2010s, when his investment firm was heavily involved in Chinese gaming companies. It’s not clear if this introduction predated Kang’s relationship and marriage to Alice, but sources close to Ms. Huang said that she was able to get close to Jensen by the 2020s. Despite being a couple, the WSJ reported that Kang seemingly accepted Alice’s relationship with Jensen, with people close to the couple saying that he would often joke that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire. Kang Wei is not just an average business executive, though. He made a name for himself in the finance world as a strategist for Shenyin Wanguo before taking over the Zhonghai Fund in 2007. This made him one of the youngest mutual fund chiefs in China at that time, before finally setting out on his own and founding Shanghai Hexi in 2010. It was also around this time that Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, entered the financial industry, first working at HSBC’s private banking arm in Hong Kong, before moving to CITIC Securities, where she attained a vice president position. It was during her time at CITIC that Alice crossed paths with Kang. Shanghai Hexi signed a deal with the securities firm in 2014 and 2015, and by 2016, corporate registry records show that Ms. Huang had joined the investment firm. The Economic Times reports Alice Huang’s move into Shanghai Hexi resulted in her getting a 25% stake in the company, all of which came from Kang. The remaining shares were shared between Kang Wei, with 48.75%, and his business partner, Zhu Xiaoming, with 26.25%, with Alice Huang’s 25% ownership stake being held through Shanghai Yuxi Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd. Meanwhile, Kang also started introducing Alice Huang as his wife to his business associates and investors. One year later, Zhu and Kang had a falling out when one of their investments under a Hexi fund resulted in a major windfall, with the two partners disagreeing on how the profits were to be shared. Nevertheless, the massive profit generated by the deal allowed Shanghai Hexi to purchase Hangzhou Shengfeng, a video game company, for around 500 million yuan from Chinese conglomerate Century Huatong. Two years after the transaction, in 2019, Hangzhou Shengfeng’s ownership was transferred to an offshore entity, which was eventually consolidated under Osmanthus Vale Holdings — a holding company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and listed Huang Le, Alice Huang’s Chinese name, as its sole owner. It was then purchased by 7Road Holdings less than two months after it was founded. While Ms. Huang was the signatory in this deal, it’s believed that she served as a “white glove,” a person who operates on behalf of another to conceal their identity — but it remains unclear if this was for Shanghai Hexi and Kang Wei or some other third party. There is not much information on Alice Huang’s activities between 2019 and 2021. However, Shanghai Hexi invested in Shanghai Longjing Information Technology, a data center-focused subsidiary of Century Huatong in 2020, where Ms. Huang served as a director between 2021 and 2022, according to a report by The Wire China . At about the same time, 7Road Holdings expanded into cloud computing, just before ChatGPT brought AI LLMs to the forefront. articles.title: Mass smuggling of up to 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs could be the underlying cause of Jensen Huang's departure, analysts claim
articles.content: Leading semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis believes that Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia may have been driven not only by revelations about his personal extramarital relationships, but also by widespread illicit exports of advanced AI accelerators to China. In its latest newsletter, analysts estimate that more than 1.5 gigawatts (GW) worth of restricted Nvidia hardware, which could be equivalent to up to 1.5 million GPUs, has reached the country despite U.S. export controls. Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained Over 1.5 GW of Nvidia hardware subject to U.S. export restrictions ultimately ended up in China in recent years, according to SemiAnalysis' Accelerator Model, which tracks AI accelerator production and destinations. The estimate excludes processors that Nvidia specifically developed to comply with U.S. export rules, such as the H20 or H800. The firm also claims that the U.S. Department of Commerce has reached a similar conclusion about the scale of unauthorized shipments. Yet, SemiAnalysis does not disclose the exact number of accelerators shipped to China illegally, or their split between Nvidia's product generations. The scale of the alleged diversions is particularly notable because modern AI accelerators require substantial power and infrastructure. While the report does not explain how it converts accelerator quantities into power figures, it is likely that the company uses package-level nameplate/rated power multiplied by the number of GPUs. Assuming that all of these AI GPUs were Nvidia H200 SXM rated for up to 700W, then China got around 2.142 million of such accelerators, while if all of these processors were B200 SXM rated for up to 1,000W, then we are talking about 1.5 million units. For a mixed deployment, the total would fall between these figures, depending on the proportion of H200 and B200 accelerators. To put these numbers into context, xAI's Colossus One had 220-230,000 Hopper H100 and H200 GPUs, whereas the Colossus 2 has a target of 1.2 million Blackwell B200 and B300 GPUs. That said, 1.5 GW of restricted Nvidia hardware in China represents an enormous amount of computing infrastructure, which is comparable, or even exceeds, the scale of xAI's entire existing Colossus operation. While SemiAnalysis did not reveal all the cases in which restricted AI accelerators reached the People's Republic of China, it supports its assessment with two well-known cases of alleged GPU smuggling. The first involves Supermicro co-founder Wally Liaw, Taiwan sales executive Steven Chang, and contractor Willy Sun, who were charged in March 2026. According to the indictment, approximately $2.5 billion worth of servers were sold to a company in Southeast Asia, with $510 million worth of equipment subsequently diverted to China and obtained by Alibaba . Prosecutors allege that the defendants used substitute servers and transferred identification labels to conceal the actual destinations of the hardware during audits. The second case involves nine individuals associated with Nvidia, Albatron, Chief Telecom, Flying Tiger, and Supermicro in Taiwan. The authorities accuse the group of arranging unauthorized exports of 130 Nvidia B300-based servers, 74 of which eventually reached China. The suspects used shell companies, forged documents, and declared Japan as the destination for servers that were actually bound for China, according to prosecutors. Taiwanese authorities discovered the operation during a drug smuggling investigation. Both cases are still before the courts. Amidst the ongoing fallout and reports into Jensen's Huang's extramarital affair with Alice…

articles.title: Pixel Weather now lets you report inaccurate weather conditions
articles.content: TL;DR The latest version of the Pixel Weather app lets you report inaccurate weather conditions. Users get to choose from a range of weather conditions and temperature options before submitting their report. This user feedback option comes amid a wave of online complaints about Pixel Weather. Google’s Pixel Weather could soon let users report inaccurate weather forecasts directly from the app. In the past, we’ve seen incidents where Pixel Weather’s data has been off the mark , and it now looks like Google is taking steps to fix that. APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship. Version 1.1.20261012 of the Pixel Weather app includes a dedicated card named Report current weather at the bottom of your current location’s weather details page. “Share the current weather condition to improve local forecasts,” the accompanying description reads.

articles.content: A Chinese company founded by Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a controversy dogging Nvidia Corp., procured smuggled AI chips that were installed at a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed International Pte, according to documents reviewed by Bloomberg News. Parmy Olson has the details. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: Grab this 8BitDo wireless controller for your gaming PC and Switch 2 at its lowest ever price, now $51.12
articles.content: A huge discount on a gamepad for your gaming PC or Nintendo Switch 2 console is available right now. You can pick up the 8BitDo Ultimate 2 game controller for only $51.12 right now , a 27% discount on a flagship wireless gamepad with precision TMR joysticks and an integrated charging dock. ● Check out this deal at Amazon This is the lowest price we've ever seen for this 8BitDo controller, according to Camelcamelcamel's data. It's important to note that there are a few different variants of this game controller that you can buy. They're pretty much identical, except for some differences in the color and button layout. This one is the cheapest right now, and it'll work with your Windows PC immediately. This is a wireless controller, and you can use it over 2.4 GHz wireless using the supplied USB adapter or via a Bluetooth connection. You can also use it wired, too, over USB. This is a Windows-compatible controller, but this particular variant of the 8BitDo Ultimate 2 is built with the Nintendo Switch in mind. It's now both Switch and Switch 2 compatible, but you'll need to update the firmware for both the controller and adapter to use it with your Switch 2. It has built-in vibration and, with those Nintendo gamers in mind, it also includes motion control functionality that you can use in-game. Ultimate 2 Bluetooth Controller for PC and Nintendo Switch: was $69.99 now $51.12 This 8BitDo Ultimate 2 wireless controller works with Windows PCs, laptops, and Nintendo Switch game consoles, with Switch 2 functionality requiring a quick firmware update. It has both linear Hall Effect and non-linear tactical triggers, which you can switch between, along with ultra-sensitive TMR joysticks, as well as a charging dock. View Deal The 8BitDo Ultimate 2 comes with both linear Hall Effect triggers and non-linear tactile triggers, with quick-switch sliders that let you choose between the two, depending on which you prefer. It's also the first 8BitDo controller on sale that uses TMR joysticks, giving you much higher sensitivity and greater precision for gaming. You can fully customize this 8BitDo controller to suit how you play. That's thanks to its Ultimate V2 software, which you can use to adjust stick and trigger precision settings, remap the buttons, adjust the RGB lighting, and set your vibration settings. It also lets you set up in-game macros, which you can activate using long presses on different keys. This is a wireless controller, so you'll need to charge its 1,000 mAh battery to keep using it (unless you decide to go wired). It comes with a charging dock, however, so you won't need to swap out any AAA batteries here. The dock works as a practical stand for your controller when you're not using it, too, and has a built-in light so you know when the charging is complete. With a sale price of $51.12, this 8BitDo Ultimate 2 wireless game controller is now at the lowest price we've ever seen it. This is a great price for a versatile controller that you can use with both your PC and Nintendo consoles, along with other devices like laptops and handheld gaming PCs like the Steam Deck, too.

articles.title: Motorola Razr Plus 2024 starts receiving Android 17, but US owners still have to wait
articles.content: TL;DR Android 17 has started rolling out to the Motorola Razr Plus 2024, beginning with its European counterpart, the Razr 50 Ultra. The update brings a redesigned Quick Settings panel, wallpaper depth effects, and a new external display clock face. US availability hasn’t been confirmed, and there’s still no verified rollout for the standard Razr 2024. Motorola is working its way backward through its Razr lineup with Android 17, and its latest stop is a two-year-old foldable. After bringing the update to the Razr 2026 and Razr 2025 families, the company has started rolling out the stable Android 17 update to the Razr Plus 2024 . There’s a small geographical catch. The update has been spotted on a European Razr 50 Ultra, which is the same phone sold in the US as the Razr Plus 2024. While there’s no confirmed US rollout yet, a stable build on its international counterpart is an encouraging sign for American owners.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge

articles.title: Here’s a demo of Google Calculator’s new Unit Conversion feature and a preview of Pixel Solver
articles.content: Credit: Stephen Schenck / Android Authority TL;DR Google announced Unit Conversion and Pixel Solver for Google Calculator with the November 2026 Pixel Drop, but the new features haven’t reached all users yet. So we managed to activate them for a look. The converter supports over 130 currencies with live exchange rates, along with everyday and technical units such as length, temperature, data, and fuel efficiency. It’s set to come to the Pixel 6a and newer in all regions. The Gemini-powered Pixel Solver (“Ask Math”) refused our queries because of its Pixel 11 exclusivity. Google recently rolled out its November 2026 Pixel Drop , headlined by a substantial upgrade to the stock Calculator app. The update adds two major features to Google Calculator: a built-in Unit Conversion module and a Gemini-powered Pixel Solver tool. As is usually the case with Google apps and updates, Google’s announcement does not directly coincide with a rollout, and many users have pointed out that they are missing the new features despite installing the November update. We got the Unit Conversion feature up and running on our test device so you can see what’s actually coming your way. APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship. Previously, converting units or checking exchange rates meant jumping out of the Calculator app and into Google Search or other third-party apps.
articles.author: Aamir Siddiqui

articles.title: Apple Launches Two Products Today
articles.content: Apple is releasing two new products today, Friday, November 13: the all-new Apple HomeView and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, both of which have been available to pre-order since mid-October. Apple HomeView : Apple's new smart home display, powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI, for entertainment and managing the home. Available in tabletop and wall-mounted models, it can recognize up to six users by face, each with a personalized Home Screen. The HomeView is priced at $299. Apple TV 4K : adds Siri AI, the A19 chip, an updated Siri Remote with Find My, and support for four-speaker surround sound with HomePod mini 2. The Apple TV 4K comes with 128GB of storage and is priced at $299. Both products were announced on October 13 alongside the HomePod mini 2, which launched October 30. As things stand, HomeView is not sold in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable on iOS in the region due to regulatory constraints. Apple has said it is "working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward," but has provided no timeline for EU availability. This article, " Apple Launches Two Products Today " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: 3 new Netflix shows you should binge-watch this weekend —including an Italian crime-mystery set in the art world (Nov. 13-15)
articles.content: November is rolling along at a concerningly fast pace, which means, if you're like us, you've probably missed some quality streaming titles these last few weeks. How exactly are you supposed to keep up with every new show arriving on top streaming services like Netflix ? Well, that's where Tom's Guide comes in: Not only will we give you a broad overview of your monthly options — here's everything coming to Netflix in November 2026 , by the way — but we also regularly curate a weekend watchlist, with three new-to-Netflix TV titles worthy of your time and attention. This weekend, that includes not one, not two, but three international gems: a German historical drama, a Rome-set newcomer that brings the murder mystery genre into the world of fine art, and a Turkish drama returning for its long-awaited second season after more than half a decade. Without further ado, here are three fresh Netflix releases you should definitely add to your weekend watchlist. 'ChiaroScuro' Love a good crime thriller? The fan-favorite genre gets an Italian accent with this Rome-set newcomer, using the Eternal City's famous galleries, museums, palaces, and churches as the backdrop for a murder investigation. When a body is chillingly discovered inside a Roman museum, staged like a famous painting by Artemisia Gentileschi, art expert Cosmo Speranza (played by Pierpaolo Spollon) and police inspector Angelo Tiberi (Andrea Lattanzi) team up as a very unlikely duo to track down the serial killer whose crimes are inspired by classic masterpieces. The case also drags Cosmo back into the mystery over the death of his father, a notorious forger who took his own life. Along with that leading pair, the cast also includes Matilde Gioli, Romana Maggiora Vergano, Aurora Giovinazzo, with Paz Vega and Alessandro Preziosi. Watch "ChiaroScuro" on Netflix now 'The Empress' season 3 The third and final chapter of the German historical drama series picks up after the Sardinian War, with Emperor Franz (Philip Froissant) deeply traumatized and taking refuge in an extramarital affair, with Empress Elisabeth (Devrim Lingnau) suffering from not only that rejection from her husband but also health issues and court pressures. Our titular heroine decides to leave Vienna for a distant coastal island where she encounters the mysterious Hungarian revolutionary Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin), with whom she shares an intense intellectual and physical attraction. Soon, Elisabeth is drawn down a path "that will forever alter her life and the future of Europe," says Netflix. Watch "The Empress" season 3 on Netflix now 'Ethos' season 2 Nearly six years after its debut season, this critically acclaimed Turkish-language drama (also known as "Bir Başkadır") returns with a follow-up from writer-director Berkun Oya. The four-episode second season brings us back to our favorite Istanbul residents, including Öykü Karayel as Meryem, Defne Kayalar as Peri, Fatih Artman as Yasin, Funda Eryiğit as Ruhiye, and Onur Saylak as Sinan. These diverse, intersecting individuals will experience "unexpected encounters and new conflicts" in the compact new season, says Netflix, with their paths continuing to intersect in the therapy room and out in the bustling city. articles.title: Google Releases TPU Sync: Open-Source KV Cache Transfer for TPUs
articles.content: Google Cloud has released TPU Sync , an open-source C++ library for moving KV caches and model weights on Cloud TPUs. The Google TPU Sync KV cache transfer library treats TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage and the data center network as one memory hierarchy. It targets a growing bottleneck: moving model state, not computing it. Google reports over 90% lower KV transfer latency on 235B to 480B parameter MoE models. TL;DR Library: Native C++ core with Python wheels for PyTorch and JAX. Tested on 235B to 480B MoE models. Runs on: Cloud TPU v7x (Ironwood) and v6e per the README . Benchmarks used TPU v7x (2x2x1), PCIe Gen5 and 200 Gbps NICs. Performance: Large cuts to KV transfer latency and time to first token (TTFT) in Google’s internal lab tests. Best: Up to 90% lower average TTFT (480B P/D serving at low concurrency, and 64K-context prefix caching). Worst: No RL numbers published. The README says it is not yet recommended for general use. Bottom line: Best: Qwen3 235B KV transfer drops from several seconds to ~230 ms. Worst: every number is self-reported and early-stage. What is TPU Sync? TPU Sync is an open-source C++ library from Google that moves TPU-tiled tensors across memory tiers with asynchronous DMA. It handles 2 jobs: KV cache state during inference, and trainer-to-sampler weight broadcast in reinforcement learning (RL). The repository is licensed Apache-2.0. How does TPU Sync work? The library spans TPU HBM, pinned host DRAM, shared storage and multi-host DCN. Storage uses experimental POSIX backends, including local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Google lists 4 design choices: Layout-preserving direct DMA: It reads JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place. Data keeps its native TPU tile layout, with no Python serialization or bounce buffers. Compute-overlapped transfers: Raw PJRT buffer aliases let transfers run during computation. Built-in DMA pacing stops large copies from delaying kernel launches. No XLA compilation in the data path: Transfers and resharding run in native C++ outside the XLA graph. High-bandwidth PCIe and DCN: It reaches up to 223 GB/s per Ironwood host, against a 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 ceiling. DCN streaming hits ~192 Gbps on 1 NIC, or ~350 Gbps across 2. Above this sit a global KV store for prefix lookups, a transfer controller and a KV cache manager. How does disaggregated prefill/decode serving use it? The prefill node offloads KV blocks to pinned host RAM through async DMA. The controller streams them host-to-host to the assigned decode node. Arriving blocks move into decode-node HBM while decoding continues. What do the TPU Sync benchmarks show? Google ran internal tests in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1). The stack was tpu-inference v0.24.0, JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1. Google team states that real-world results will vary. For P/D disaggregated serving: KV transfer overhead fell by over 90%. Qwen3 235B median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds to ~230 ms. Average TTFT fell 60% for 235B and 90% for 480B at low concurrency. Token output throughput rose 30% to 70% for 235B during traffic spikes. For prefix caching: Effective cache capacity grew by an order of magnitude when MoE weights fill most of HBM. Average TTFT fell by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads. Throughput rose over 50%, and P99 inter-token latency fell 30%. Which frameworks does TPU Sync support? TPU Sync integrates with PyTorch through TorchTPU and with JAX natively. In vLLM-TorchTPU , it is the TPU KV connector behind vLLM’s KVConnector interface. In SGLang-TorchTPU , it is the P/D transfer backend and hierarchical cache I/O backend. On GKE, llm-d 1.0 uses it for prefix-cache-affinity routing and experimental spill to Managed Lustre. Inferact and RadixArk co-engineered the vLLM and SGLang integrations. Google says Meta and Wayfair are evaluating the architecture. How does TPU Sync compare with GPU-side alternatives? articles.title: 1994 Jeep Cherokee owner hacks 32-year-old car with Claude AI to pass California smog tests
articles.content: An AI enthusiast managed to get his old 1994 Jeep Cherokee to pass the California smog tests, all thanks to the help of AI and a little electronics wiring skill. This 32-year-old car had only a primitive engine computer, but after connecting it to a laptop via an Arduino Nano board, many settings could be read and eventually controlled. The above video documents Muhammad Zulali’s journey from the Jeep failing consecutive smog tests, to managing to hook it up and get readings from the ECU, to tuning and fixing the engine emission issues. All the while, Claude provided guidance, and Codex wrote any required code. This rather old Jeep was failing the California smog tests due to producing too much NOx at certain test speeds. It initially failed at 25mph. Then, after Zulali made some adjustments to the oxygen mix, it failed at both 25mph and 50mph. Yes, it got worse. Zulali admits he was effectively making adjustments blind, and subsequent regulatory pollution tests cost nearly $100 each time. That’s clearly a big problem, but we have AI to help us in 2026. Actually, it was AI and a $3 microcontroller, contributing to a total bill of materials of no more than $15. The first hurdle facing the possible AI solution was the question of how to interface an old car and a new laptop. Claude told the Jeep owner that the engine communicated on a Chrysler SCI bus at ~7,800 baud, which was electrically inverted compared to a typical serial port. An Arduino Nano can handle the required inversion and hook up the data to a modern computer. The Nano was breadboarded , with a few necessary wires, three of which connected to the 6-pin diagnostic plug in the Cherokee. (Image credit: Muhammad Zulali ) The first connection attempt was a success, but only coolant temperature and battery voltage were charted by the system to begin with. Zulali wanted more data points plus some controls to fix the smog test problem. After a couple of red herrings regarding the engine “running rich” with 22% extra fuel, based on other car model data, the Jeep owner got Claude to collect data from test drives. The AI logged engine data and fault codes during a drive at 25 mph and at 50 mph to see what was happening. It was also let loose to control things like fuel pressure. With what looked like a credible diagnosis and solution in hand, Zulali wanted to reflash the car’s main ECU with AI-tweaked code that would mean it could pass all the California smog tests. Unfortunately, this car’s computer was just a few months too old to feature reflashable firmware. Instead, the Jeep owner got Codex to inject and run custom code inside a nearby EEPROM . “Claude did most of the diagnostic work and Codex did pretty much all of the memory work,” admits Zulali. “I just did the wiring and the driving.” He added that he didn’t need the services of a mechanic or a Chrysler dealer tool for this feat. In addition to the video, the Cherokee emissions fixer has created a GitHub repository for this project, dubbed xj-scanner . It is free software distributed under the GPLv3 license.

articles.title: The five-minute stainless steel reset that makes a tired kitchen look new
articles.content: If you are getting your home ready for festive hosting, do not overlook the sink. Even with pristine worktops and clean floors, cloudy stainless steel covered in chalky water rings instantly makes a kitchen feel tired. Before the holiday cooking frenzy begins, you can revive a dull basin without scratching the metal or buying pricey specialty cleaners. This five-minute routine cuts through greasy buildup and seals in a bright, showroom shine just in time for visitors. Cut through grease with warm soapy water Rinse away loose food debris, then wash the entire basin thoroughly with hot water and dish soap. Using a soft microfiber cloth or non-scratch sponge, wipe in long, steady strokes that follow the faint brushed grain of the steel rather than scrubbing in circles. (Image credit: Shutterstock) This removes the surface grease film so your cleaning paste can make direct contact with the mineral spots underneath. Lift cloudy limescale with baking soda Sprinkle a light dusting of baking soda over the damp steel , concentrating on the drain and faucet base where hard water residue gathers. Using a damp cloth, work the powder into a paste along the metal's grain to lift dull water rings without scratching. For stubborn hard-water marks, rinse the baking soda paste away thoroughly first, then apply a light spray of white vinegar directly to the mineral scale . (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Letting the vinegar sit undiluted for a few minutes allows its mild acetic acid to chemically dissolve crusty calcium and magnesium deposits without being neutralized by the alkaline baking soda. Avoid spraying vinegar onto specialized faucet finishes like matte black, brass, or oil-rubbed bronze, as the acid can strip or discolor the coating. Once the mineral scale softens, use a soft-bristled brush or non-scratch sponge to gently agitate and lift any remaining gritty buildup from the metal’s surface texture. Buff dry and seal the shine Standing water left to evaporate is why cloudy spots return. Use a dry dish towel or microfiber cloth to wipe the entire basin, faucet, and drainboard until completely dry. For an optional finishing shine, a pply a single drop of mineral oil (like baby oil) or olive oil to a soft cloth and buff it into the steel , following the direction of the metal's grain. Buff vigorously with a clean, dry section of the towel until no residue remains. (Image credit: Shutterstock) This creates a light barrier that repels water beads and keeps the shine lasting longer, especially on faucets and handles. articles.title: Netflix’s new mystery thriller movie is guaranteed to be No. 1 this weekend — but Jessica Chastain deserves better
articles.content: A country music superstar, a missing rising star and the darker side of Nashville make for an intriguing setup, especially when you’ve got an Oscar-winning actress leading the investigation. That's the premise behind “Heartland,” Netflix's latest original thriller, starring Jessica Chastain as a retired country music legend. The film is written and directed by Shana Feste, who previously explored the country music scene in 2010's “Country Strong.” This time though, she's trading the musical drama for a mystery thriller. Tom's Guide Verdict: 'Heartland' Rating: 2/5 Verdict: "Heartland" starts with an intriguing mystery and some strong country music credentials, but Jessica Chastain's Netflix thriller loses its way after a predictable halfway twist. There's some Nashville charm here, but the payoff disappoints. Where to watch: "Heartland" is streaming on Netflix In “Heartland,” Chastain plays Misty Jones, a former country music megastar who has spent 20 years away from Nashville and the spotlight. However, when her niece Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), an up-and-coming country singer, suddenly goes missing, Misty returns to her old hometown to find her. Her investigation quickly draws her into Nashville’s murkier corners, where she encounters a number of potential suspects: Charlie’s boyfriend Jace (Ross Lynch) and manager Roy Combs (Garrett Hedlund). Along the way, Misty also finds herself confronting some uncomfortable truths about her own past. I’ve already watched “Heartland,” and while its premise certainly caught my attention, I’m not entirely convinced the finished movie delivers everything it promises. So, is this latest Netflix original worth adding to your watchlist, or are we looking at another forgettable thriller from the streamer? Here are my honest thoughts and whether I’d recommend giving it a watch this weekend. ‘Heartland’ hits the right notes with its music, not its mystery (Image credit: Tina Rowden / Netflix) “Heartland” gets off to a pretty jarring start, with Misty ending up in a heated disagreement with her neighbor over her dogs. I understand what the movie is going for here, using the confrontation to establish Misty’s closed-off nature and aggressive streak, but it’s an unusual way to introduce the character and didn’t immediately win me over. Still, like many of Netflix’s original movies, the first half is where “Heartland” is at its strongest. We get straight into the mystery surrounding Charlie’s disappearance, with Misty’s brother pleading for her to return to Nashville after Charlie has missed several shows and concerts, leaving fans to drag her name through the mud online. Returning to her hometown also brings plenty of painful memories to the surface, with quick, scattered flashbacks offering glimpses into the trauma she’s spent years trying to bury. Chastain gives a strong enough performance, but I struggled to connect with Misty, which made it harder to invest in her personal journey. It was the mystery surrounding her niece that kept me interested. (Image credit: Tina Rowden / Netflix) Unfortunately, that mystery doesn’t have quite the staying power the movie needs. A major twist arrives around the halfway point, and rather than giving the story a much-needed boost, it pretty much sucks the intrigue out of the second half. Once the reveal comes into focus, there’s very little left to keep you guessing, particularly if you’ve been paying attention to how certain characters are introduced and positioned throughout the opening act. I had a pretty good idea of where things were heading from early on, so the eventual reveal didn’t carry much of a punch. It’s a shame, because the first half does enough to make you curious about what’s really going on, but the film struggles to maintain that momentum once its biggest secret is out in the open. articles.content: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR A regulatory filing has revealed that the Motorola Signature 27 is available in two models, with each having a different battery capacity. The standard phone has a rated capacity of 6,790mAh, while the downgraded model has a rated capacity of 5,350mAh. It’s not clear which countries will receive the Signature 27 with a smaller battery. Update: November 13, 2026 (6:26 AM ET): It looks like Motorola was indeed planning to offer a Signature 27 with a 5,500mAh battery in some markets. The phone’s product page mentioned a smaller battery in markets like Germany and the UK (see first screenshot below), but this has subsequently been updated to only mention a 7,000mAh battery. In fact, Google still mentions a 5,500mAh battery, as seen in the second image below. We’ve asked Motorola for clarity regarding this battery situation and will update our article accordingly. Here’s hoping the Signature 27 is available with a 7,000mAh battery in all markets.

articles.title: Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests
articles.content: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used. According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing. The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation. It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards. Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence. In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken. "We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action. "Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent." Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning." Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system. However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries. The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted. The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes. Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high. Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute , as well as the King's College London Policy Institute , showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively. Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience. The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition. Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns. "Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said. "A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence." As…

articles.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
articles.content: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it . The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough . Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy. The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however. The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants. Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain…

articles.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
articles.content: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its…

articles.title: macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64
articles.content: The eternal spiral of computing gets yet another loop. Apple introduced its own Arm-based chips in 2020, surprising the world with a series of SoCs with a particularly high power-to-watt ratio, a perfect fit for the company's quality portables. As the designs improved on raw performance, Apple shifted away from Intel-based Macs. That meant that enterprising hackers who ran macOS on their PCs could no longer do so — until today, thanks to the Stela Apple Silicon translation layer . Stela is a minty-fresh new project from Tyler Smith, and it's just gotten started, with three releases since the first 0.1 version in barely half a day. The author warns that "it is slow and not very stable," but those warnings are somehow invisible to techies trying out a new toy. For practical purposes, Stela is a Linux-based UEFI application for loading macOS 27, presenting a virtual M2 Mac Mini to the operating system. The developer answered a couple of questions in the project's Discord server , and he remarked that the macOS image to be used is not modified at all: "Stela provides the translation and hardware behavior underneath that lets macOS go through the exact same restore process you might do on a real Mac." The server has seen a substantial influx of users, many of them posting photos of their PCs near-booting macOS. Predictably, most of the questions were about supporting their own particular hardware, but the excitement is palpable. To get started, all you need is to download Stela from the release pages , provide a USB stick to then boot your PC with, and, naturally, your own copy of macOS. Stela will take care of translating AArch instructions into x86-64. The translation layer uses a combination of ahead-of-time and just-in-time (JIT) compilation for the CPU, and translates Apple's Metal graphics layer calls to Mesa's NIR instructions. The hardware requirements are basically potato-level, requiring only an x86-64-v2 — a 2008 Intel Core chip, or a 2011-vintage AMD FX processor. The author mentions that AVX2 and AVX-512 "are used when present," but woe betide you if your processor is that old to begin with. You'll need 8 GB of RAM, UEFI support, a GPT partition or entire drive, and an Nvidia card from the 16xx series to present-day 5000 models. There's no Wi-Fi support yet, and Bluetooth is limited, but the list of working Ethernet controllers is extensive, covering models from Intel, Realtek, Broadcom, Aquantia, Atheros, and even USB Ethernet sticks. The author says that he intends for Stela to eventually support all the hardware the Linux kernel does. Purely hypothetically, with AI automation, it's not completely insane to think that much of macOS could be pre-translated to x86-64. Yet such an endeavor has many caveats, namely the fact that a lot of code, like a browser's JIT JavaScript compilation, doesn't exist on the disk image to begin with. There's also the fact that no matter how efficient a translation layer is, the OS still needs to cryptographically accept it and run it, perhaps requiring further modification still. But we can, in fact, dream of ditching Windows for macOS without being tied to Apple's pricey and barely-repairable hardware.
