articles.title: This Texas rocket builder’s high-tech ring of fire could revolutionize aerospace
articles.content: One early morning in May 2025 at Spaceport America, a desert basin on the outskirts of Las Cruces, New Mexico, a silver rocket shot through the air. Launches aren’t a rare occurrence at the commercial launch site, but this test flight wasn’t an everyday event. A century after Robert Goddard launched his first liquid-fueled rocket , the flight by Venus Aerospace, a Texas-based startup, may have heralded a new kind of rocket, a new technology, and maybe a new era. “It’s a step change in combustion physics,” says Sarah Duggleby, a Venus Aerospace cofounder along with her husband, Andrew Duggleby, a rocket engineer. The rocket launch represented the first successful U.S. flight of a rotating detonation rocket engine (RDRE). Venus predicts this tech—which harnesses a continuous detonation wave around a ring-shaped chamber, generating increased thrust with less fuel—can achieve hypersonic flight. The startup has seen interest in its technology soar at a time when spending on defense, commercial space development, and aerospace technology is rapidly accelerating. Duggleby estimates that Venus RDRE rockets can double the payload that rockets can take into space. [Photo: Venus Aerospace] “It turns out when you build the most efficient liquid rocket engine in the world, defense and space companies start coming to you like, ‘Hey, could you sell us engines?’” she says. “We’ve pivoted, but at the core, it’s always been about, if you want to go fast, you need a new engine.” The company has raised just shy of $140 million, including a $91 million Series B this June, and employs 113 people, per PitchBook. It struck a development deal with Lockheed Martin this past summer to integrate RDRE tech into precision long-range missiles. [Animation: Venus Aerospace] In 2018, Andrew Duggleby was a Navy Reserve officer and the family was stationed in Japan. He and Sarah realized they wouldn’t be able to make it home for a grandmother’s birthday. Andrew joked that while it was going to be an excruciating 13 hours to fly home to the States, there was a new rocket engine technology being developed that could theoretically do the flight in an hour. They laughed, but the idea stuck with them, and they founded Venus two years later. The rocket he was talking about was the RDRE. Theorized since the 1980s and finally cracked by a team of researchers from Purdue University and University of Central Florida , RDRE relies on a precisely timed ring of subsonic explosions, calibrated and choreographed to very rapidly detonate in a circular pattern, creating more thrust with less fuel use. Traditional rocket engines, from the Saturn V to SpaceX’s Falcon, rely on a combustion process called deflagration, where a flame is exposed to a mixture of fuel and oxidizers. To put it simply: traditional rockets involve a continuous burn, RDRE rockets involve a series of explosions, Sarah Duggleby said an RDRE launch even sounds different; she can tell when a test flight is successful when it hits a certain whistling sound. Venus’s rockets have achieved 15% more energy efficiency than the Saturn V, the rocket that launched astronauts to the moon in the ‘60s and ‘70s. For comparison, the new SpaceX rockets are just 2% more efficient than their Saturn forebears, Duggleby says. The Dugglebys were both working for Virgin Orbit when Sarah read a news item about university researchers proving this new type of engine. In June of 2020, the couple decided to take the leap, quit Virgin, and pursue development of a high-speed plane using this new RDRE technology. They chose the Houston Spaceport for the combination of aerospace talent and facilities; currently, from their headquarters at the spaceport, they can test-fire mounted rocket engines right outside their hangar door at Ellington Field. articles.title: The hidden costs of repurposing laptops
articles.content: Keeping pace with evolving technology demands is an increasing challenge for businesses . Software licenses and tool sprawl rapidly eat into technology budgets so when it comes to hardware, it’s perhaps unsurprising that there is a tendency to extend the lifecycle of products, rather than replace them. One example of this is repurposing old laptops into thin clients. In simple terms, a thin client is a device that runs services and software from a centralized server, allowing users to access their desktop environment from any device with an internet connection. This cloud-based approach removes the need for very powerful, and often costly devices as most of the computing power and storage remains on the server. This method is intended to extend the machine lifecycle, removing the up-front cost of new hardware and when budgets are tight or profits are stagnating, this can feel like a huge win. It can also seem like a more sustainable choice for companies on paper. For leaders concerned about e-waste, repurposing laptops may appear to be the right choice for the environment, and for their business. Seems perfect, right? Unfortunately, this is not always the case. Reusing existing hardware is not the same as extending a system’s lifecycle and delaying the purchase of a dedicated thin client doesn't remove that investment, it simply shifts it into a series of smaller, less visible costs. Over time, repairs, support, downtime and higher energy consumption can leave businesses spending more than if they had invested in purpose-built hardware from the outset. Why repurposing is on the rise In Europe, virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) devices, which are used to connect to a virtual or cloud desktop instead of running everything locally, make up a significant share of the market. Of that chunk, only around half are dedicated thin-client hardware (purpose-built boxes or all-in-one units). Pressure to reduce IT costs, extend hardware lifecycles and meet sustainability quotas often lead businesses to assume that repurposing is the best move. And, as processing moves to the cloud, or a VDI server, local performance inside laptops matters less. The device on the desk essentially becomes a display responsible for capturing keyboard and mouse input and maintaining a network connection. Since the laptop is now primarily acting as a gateway to cloud -hosted applications, it can appear that the hardware itself no longer needs to be particularly capable. But this fails to acknowledge one fundamental point. The physical laptop is still at the end of its refresh cycle, and its components are still ageing. Instead of making the most of the tech they already have, leaders should be considering whether that approach makes the most sense in the long term. Ultimately, it doesn’t - a dedicated thin client delivers both architectural and financial advantages over a 10-year lifecycle, with lower maintenance, reduced energy use and a significantly lower total cost of ownership. Is an ageing laptop the most reliable and sustainable endpoint? Repurposing old laptops is a one-time delay strategy, not a permanent infrastructure model. Take a 4-year-old laptop, for example. This device will have a battery operating at 50% capacity... or worse. Even if it gets updated with a fast, low-resource system designed to run smoothly on older or weaker computers, such as a lightweight Linux OS, that battery will swell, fail, or die completely within 12-24 months. Replacing laptop batteries or having employees tethered to power outlets entirely undermines one of the key benefits of thin clients: low maintenance Laptops also have various moving parts, like cooling fans and hinges, along with highly fragile components such as keyboards, trackpads and screens. In contrast, hardware thin clients are built with solid-state components specifically intended to last 8-10 years without a single physical failure. articles.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen: 2.5x Faster Than Gemini 3.8 Flash
articles.content: Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen , a fast model for coding and agentic work. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is a proprietary model from Google DeepMind built for everyday agent loops. It sits below the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon . Google calls it its “daily driver for agentic workflows.” TL;DR Size: 1,048,576-token unified window for input, thinking and output. Runs on: Google-hosted API only. No weights, no quantized variants, no self-hosting. Serving hardware not disclosed. Performance: Scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at high, above Argon’s 50. Best: 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, versus 18.2% for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Worst: Ranks only #5 on Agent Arena. Costs 2x Gemini 3.8 Flash’s current introductory price. Bottom line: Best: frontier-class agent scores at $1.50/$7.50 per 1M tokens. Worst: closed, and synchronous output caps at 65,536 tokens. What is Gemini 4 Hydrogen? Hydrogen is a closed-weights model served through the Gemini API and Google products. The model card says it is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count, architecture or training hardware. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Input covers text, images, audio, video, PDFs, tables and charts, per the What’s New guide . Output is text. The 1M window is shared by input, thinking and output tokens. How do the 4 thinking levels work? Developers set thinking_level inside generation_config . Values are low , medium , high and a new xhigh . The default is high , not medium as on 3.8 Flash. A minimal setting now returns an error. The model card warns that higher levels use more tokens. How does Hydrogen work with Carbon and Argon? The key design idea is role-splitting across models. In Google Antigravity , an Orchestrator option switches models inside 1 task. Carbon explores, resolves ambiguity and plans. Hydrogen edits files, updates packages and runs tests. When Hydrogen hits friction, it hands control back to Carbon. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, this pairing reached near-Carbon task success rates. It used 24% less quota and finished 19% faster than Carbon alone. The Antigravity SDK exposes the same split for custom multi-agent systems. How does Gemini 4 Hydrogen perform on benchmarks? All figures are self-reported by Google unless noted. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index : 51 at high, 54 at xhigh. Argon scores 50 on Index v5.0 . Terminal-Bench 4.1 : 57%, versus 18.2% for 3.8 Flash. HLE-Diamond: 58.8%, leading its class. Vals Tax Agent Bench : 52.3%, ranked #1 overall. Vals Legal Research Bench : 55.8%, tied for #1. Multimodal Knowledge Agent : 53.4%. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 : 71.6%. Agent Arena : ranked #5. Speed is the headline claim. Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash at the default high level. In partner tests, it ran 2x to 2.8x faster with 12% to 23% fewer tokens. Google also reports more than 5x fewer fabricated claims than 3.8 Flash. It scored 96.7% on an internal agent honesty evaluation. It was 2.3x more resilient to indirect prompt injection on Gray Swan’s benchmark. How much does Gemini 4 Hydrogen cost? The API price is $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens. Pricing is flat across the full window. Output pricing includes thinking tokens. Implicit caching cuts input to $0.075 per 1M for prompts of 4,096 tokens or more. Explicit caching is not supported. The price context matters. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs $0.75/$3.75 until December 31, 2026. From January 1, 2027, it rises to $1.50/$7.50, matching Hydrogen. Argon costs $2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20. Where can developers use Gemini 4 Hydrogen? The model ID is gemini-4-hydrogen . It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio on all tiers, and Android Studio. It also ships in Gemini for business , the Gemini app, Google Search and Sheets. Antigravity access requires Google AI Pro or Ultra. Vertex AI is not mentioned in the launch posts. articles.title: Palantir's NHS cancer app gets plenty of praise, precious few users
articles.content: Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting. Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment. Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use. In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent. The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP. Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients. In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer . Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here . In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request . It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months. However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply. Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year. The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy. One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app. No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it. East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response . In its FoI response , Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements. Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app. In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP. Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient…

articles.title: Skip the novelty junk: genius kitchen gadget gifts under $50 they’ll actually use
articles.content: Kitchen gadgets can take the hassle and mess out of dinner, provided you choose the right ones. Love cooking curries? An electric grinder will make preparing spice blends a breeze. Enjoy salads? A vegetable chopper will let you dice vegetables far more quickly than using a knife. Have a tiny kitchen? A mini food processor will fit in even the smallest corner. Personally I'm a big fan of anything that keeps the smell of garlic off my hands, so a silicone garlic peeler and dishwasher-safe chopper are two of my favorites. I also love my coffee, and I always turn to my trusty AeroPress if I'm not in the mood to spend time making espresso. The right gadget can be a game-changer, and makes a truly thoughtful Christmas gift when you know what kind of dishes your loved one enjoys preparing. Here I've rounded up a collection of top quality kitchen helpers that your friends and family will use daily — all under $50. articles.content: Original Mass Effect composer Jack Wall says his inspiration comes mostly from "visuals" that "feel like an embarrassment of riches that inform how I write" Wall also shares the specific characteristics that helped shape Mass Effect 1 and 2 's soundtrack and the "groundbreaking" tools he used He says that for Mass Effect 2 , he used Wwise (Wave Works Interactive Sound Engine) to implement the score into the game, which was "far superior" to Mass Effect 1 Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 composer Jack Wall has revealed the "groundbreaking" tools he used to create each game's iconic soundtrack. In an interview with TechRadar Gaming , where he explained what makes Mass Effect 's iconic music so different from other sci-fi and role-playing games (RPGs), Wall said he typically finds the best inspiration from simply observing visuals, which helps inform the project's direction. "As a composer, I see all games, TV series, or Movies as completely unique and special," he said. "I get inspired by the visuals, and honestly those visuals feel like an embarrassment of riches that inform how I write." According to Wall, Mass Effect has very specific characteristics that helped shape the game's atmosphere: "Sound, theme (melody), and vibe." "That’s pretty much it. All specific to Mass Effect, of course. I suppose you could say this about any medium you write for as a composer," he said, adding that instruments like "Moog synths and other analog synths," as well as "orchestra, voices, some specific percussion, lots of arpeggiated synths with orchestra on top," were also things he gravitated towards for the first two games. Wall also discussed the inspirations for Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 's core sound and themes , explaining that game director Casey Hudson "wanted to play with 80s synth mixed with quasi-orchestra" music, which was the basis for the series' memorable vibe. As for how he captured that sound, the composer said, "For ME1 , we used analog modeled plugins from Arturia and other companies," which was unheard of during the game's development. "At the time, it was pretty groundbreaking stuff," Wall recalled, "and just made it possible to recall settings immediately for addressing different versions of the same piece or reuse for related cues later on. The real Moog synths are notoriously tough to recall." However, for Mass Effect 2 , he used Wwise (Wave Works Interactive Sound Engine) to implement the score into the game, which "was a game changer for us" since they didn't have the tool for the first game. "I think the way the music plays back in ME2 is far superior to ME1 ," Wall added.
articles.author: Demi Williams

articles.title: Packaging Innovation for Good
articles.content: The European Union has declared an ultimatum against unsustainability: all consumer packaging placed on the EU market must be designed for recycling by 2030. This mandate was announced by the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) and formally became law in all 27 EU member states on Aug. 12, 2026. Since then, the mandate has placed restrictions on synthetic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) in food packaging as part of the “Design for Recycling” (DfR) framework, which will become the baseline by 2030. It is significantly reshaping how companies design, import and sell products globally. All packaged products must meet these regulatory changes, not just those manufactured in the EU. Because many brands prefer to standardize packaging across different nations’ markets, it is probable that PPWR’s influence will reach well beyond Europe as brands change their designs to streamline operations. Under PPWR, materials will be graded based on their recyclability performance rates through the DfR framework. Grade A materials are __ ≥95% recyclable __and meet the highest circular life cycle standards. Grade B materials are ≥80% recyclable and are still considered to be highly efficient. Materials graded as C are ≥70% recyclable. Any material rated below 70% is deemed unrecyclable and will be banned from all markets. The new rules imply that paperboard is one of the best materials for long-term reuse, reducing and recycling because it combines a high recyclability rate and excellent compatibility with set content targets. This paper-based material can be recycled 5-10 times into innovative packaging for consumer retailers and their customers. After it is responsibly disposed of, the cycle starts again for this valuable material. European waste systems reportedly recover 87% of paper and paperboard packaging for reuse. This significantly outperforms plastic, which has just a 42% recovery rate . Other fiber-based materials help companies adjust to the tightening restrictions and mandates on single-use plastic packaging while simultaneously supporting enduring goals made for resource efficiency and overall recyclability. The first rising concern about single-use plastics began in the 2010s. By 2022, the European Commission proposed PPWR to replace the outdated Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (PPWD) of 1994. By February 2025, PPWR went into full effect. In the coming years, the development of secondary legislation will start. By 2028, mandatory standardized labels will appear on consumer packaging and on all waste sorting receptacles. Later on in the early 2030s, all packaging in the EU, whether locally produced or imported, will officially meet DfR criteria. Most plastic packaging and plastic parts will meet initial minimum recycled content requirements. By the end of the decade, all packaging must meet even stricter criteria for recyclability to ensure an even more sustainable world. The PPWR intends to set a binding packaging waste reduction target of 15% by 2040 . Brands that adapt to the DfR mandates from the start by adopting paperboard material and designing for a circular material lifecycle will be better prepared for decades to come. Additionally, they will also gain an advantage in a competitive market where environmental sustainability is rapidly becoming the criterion.

articles.title: GITEX GLOBAL 2026 Puts AI Security, Cyber Resilience and Post-Quantum Readiness in Focus
articles.content: As artificial intelligence moves from experimentation into critical business and government infrastructure, cybersecurity is facing a new set of challenges. Autonomous AI agents, increasingly interconnected systems, and growing concerns around data sovereignty are changing how organizations approach digital security. These developments will take center stage at GITEX GLOBAL 2026 , taking place December 7–11 in Dubai, UAE. With a dedicated cybersecurity showcase, GITEX is bringing together global cybersecurity companies, government institutions, technology leaders, and industry experts to explore the next generation of digital defense. Explore GITEX GLOBAL 2026: Register here. GITEX Cyber Valley: Addressing the Next Generation of Cyber Threats One of the key cybersecurity highlights of this year's event is GITEX Cyber Valley , which will focus on AI security, dual-use cyber technologies, and post-quantum readiness. As organizations increasingly deploy AI agents capable of making decisions and executing tasks, questions around accountability, access control, and operational security are becoming more urgent. The challenge is no longer limited to protecting networks and endpoints. Organizations must also secure the data, infrastructure, and autonomous systems that increasingly power their operations. GITEX Cyber Valley will bring these conversations together through tailored business meetings and private briefings for global cybersecurity leaders, creating opportunities to examine how organizations can scale AI capabilities while protecting the systems and information they depend on. Global Cybersecurity Leaders Take the Stage GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will feature an extensive lineup of cybersecurity companies showcasing technologies and solutions across the security ecosystem. Confirmed cybersecurity exhibitors include Acronis, AMIVIZ, Cohesity, Commvault, Forcepoint, Forescout, Kaspersky, ManageEngine, NETSCOUT, Netskope, NinjaOne, Proofpoint, SentinelOne / Sentinel Labs, and Trellix. Their participation reflects the breadth of the cybersecurity landscape, spanning data protection, endpoint security, network defense, threat detection, and enterprise resilience. The UAE Cybersecurity Council will also participate, alongside other government institutions and public-sector entities, highlighting the importance of collaboration between national cybersecurity strategies and private-sector innovation. Why AI Is Changing the Cybersecurity Conversation The growing adoption of AI is creating new opportunities for businesses, but it is also expanding the attack surface. AI-powered applications, autonomous agents, cloud infrastructure, and connected systems introduce new security considerations. Organizations must account for how AI systems access information, interact with other applications, and operate within critical business environments. At the same time, the emergence of quantum computing is prompting organizations to consider the long-term resilience of their encryption and data protection strategies. These developments make AI security and post-quantum readiness increasingly important areas of discussion for cybersecurity professionals, technology providers, and government decision-makers. GITEX GLOBAL's wider focus on sovereign AI, frontier models, agentic AI, and sovereign security provides a broader context for these discussions, connecting cybersecurity with the infrastructure and technologies shaping the next phase of digital transformation. GITEX Global 2026: A Global Meeting Point for Technology and Cybersecurity Beyond its cybersecurity programme, GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will bring together more than 6,000 global technology enterprises, government entities, and startups, alongside 1000+ investors representing nearly US$2 trillion in assets under management. articles.title: Postgres not using your index? It's counting pages, not rows
articles.content: Slow Postgres, part 1 of 8. The SQL and raw numbers for every test are on GitHub . A Seq Scan reads each page once, in order. An index lookup walks the B-tree and then reads one heap page per TID. You add an index on status , run EXPLAIN , and Postgres reads the whole table anyway. ANALYZE doesn't change the plan. Someone suggests SET enable_seqscan = off , the plan finally shows your index, and the query gets slower. Usually the planner is right. It prices a plan by the 8 KB pages it has to read and by whether it reads them in order or jumps around between them, and once you count pages the same way, you can answer most "why is it ignoring my index" tickets yourself. This series started as my notes from an open lesson on slow Postgres queries by balun.courses. The tests and numbers are my own. One note before the numbers: the AlphaVPS link at the end is a referral link, so I may get a commission at no extra cost to you, and the netcup vouchers come from my own account. The short version: Postgres prices a plan in pages, and in my test table a status with 0.9% of the rows sits on 94% of them, so its index saves 12 page reads out of 221. On 5 million rows in RAM, the index beat a full scan up to 10% of the rows when the matches were scattered, and at every share I tried (up to 50%) when they were stored together. Read cold from disk, the scattered lookups at 0.5% and 1% of rows ran 2 to 5 times slower than a full scan, and Postgres still picked them. A 200-row table gets a Seq Scan even when 2 rows match, so a plan from a tiny test copy says nothing about production. Keep enable_seqscan out of app code, read pg_stats before CREATE INDEX , and if you only query the rare values, index only those rows. What a B-tree index stores A regular B-tree index keeps only keys, the values it is sorted by, and next to each key a TID: the row's address in the heap, which is the table's main storage. A TID is a page number plus a slot on that page. You can see it as the hidden ctid column: SELECT ctid, id, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'chargeback' ORDER BY id LIMIT 3; ctid | id | status ---------+------+------------ (7,48) | 1000 | chargeback (14,96) | 2000 | chargeback (22,8) | 3000 | chargeback Row 1000 is slot 48 on page 7. An index lookup for 'chargeback' returns a list of addresses like these, and Postgres then visits each of those heap pages to fetch the row and check that your transaction can see it. The second step is the one people forget. To fetch one row, Postgres has to read the whole 8 KB page it sits on. The lab: 30,000 orders on 221 pages The lab runs on PostgreSQL 17.11 in Docker with default settings. My numbers come from a 4-vCPU, 8 GB cloud VM, but any small VPS or a laptop will do. CREATE TABLE orders ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL, amount_cents int NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL ); INSERT INTO orders (created_at, amount_cents, status) SELECT now() - (30000 - i) * interval '1 minute', (random() * 10000)::int, CASE WHEN i % 1000 = 0 THEN 'chargeback' -- 30 rows, 0.1% WHEN i % 100 = 0 THEN 'failed' -- 270 rows, 0.9% WHEN i % 10 = 0 THEN 'created' -- 2,700 rows, 9% ELSE 'paid' -- 27,000 rows, 90% END FROM generate_series(1, 30000) AS i; CREATE INDEX orders_status_idx ON orders (status); ANALYZE orders; SELECT relpages, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders'; relpages | reltuples ----------+----------- 221 | 30000 136 rows fit on a page, so 30,000 rows take 221 pages. I picked 30,000 because ANALYZE samples 300 × default_statistics_target rows, which is 30,000 at the default. On this table it reads every row, so the statistics are exact and your plans should come out the same as mine. articles.title: Tech Adoption Is a Cultural Problem: Why UX Habits Beat Innovation
articles.content: "You’re using our platform wrong." Oh no, sweetheart. Culture doesn’t adapt to your technology. Stop blaming Mercury in retrograde when users refuse to abandon their old habits for your shiny new tool. The pattern is always the same: the best tool in the room loses to the one people already trust. Founders file this failure under pricing, onboarding, or "users who need education." In reality, it belongs under culture. My name is Daria . I help tech companies explain what makes their products different and why they matter. At university, I studied sociology and cultural studies. It taught me to look at people in groups first, and products second. Look at the current wave of AI: the Humane AI Pin had stellar backers, deep pockets, and massive hype. It was dead in a year. ChatGPT was a plain text box, and it became the fastest-growing app in history. Same period, same underlying tech, and culture decided which one survived. The best tool loses to the habit people trust In 2020, a Japanese minister went to war on two office objects: the fax machine and the hanko, the small personal seal people stamp in red ink instead of signing. Taro Kono (Minister for Digital Transformation of Japan) had the power and the better technology. A signed PDF is faster, cheaper, and easier to search than a stamped fax. He got most government offices to agree to drop the seal. Years later, the fax still hums and the seal still sits in the drawer. The seal survived because in Japan it was never only a tool. It stands for identity and consent. A company, a bank, and a neighbor all read it the same way. A better tool cannot push out a habit the whole country trusts. In China , credit cards never caught on; by 2021 only about 38 percent of adults had one. So people skipped the card and went from cash straight to the QR code. Today two apps, Alipay and WeChat Pay , handle more than nine in ten mobile payments, from the fruit stall to the temple donation box. The same thing happens inside companies now. A team gets a powerful new AI tool, and people keep working the old way, because the old way is the one they trust. The Chat GPT UX miracle How did ChatGPT manage to become so popular and usher in a new era of consumer AI? People already knew how to type a question into a box, the way they type into Google or a chat with a friend. More than a million people tried it in five days. Around 100 million were using it two months after launch. TikTok took nine months to reach that number. Instagram took more than two years. ChatGPT did not ask us to adopt a new habit or buy a new device. The company didn't ruin our familiar flow. Strong tech can still read the room wrong The Humane AI Pin launched in 2024 with huge attention. It clipped to your shirt, had no screen, and answered out loud or showed tiny text on your palm. To use it, people had to wear a new device, learn new hand gestures, and talk to their own chest in public. By the summer, the company was taking back more pins each day than it sold. In 2025, HP bought what was left for 116 million dollars and switched the pins off. The Rabbit R1 , another AI gadget from the same year, got the same cold response. Both asked people to build a habit from zero, with nothing pushing them to do it. Great tech can still misjudge the culture it lands in. In February 2024, Google added image generation to Gemini. Asked for pictures of people from history, it often returned images that did not match the record. The reaction was loud and fast. Within days, Google paused the feature for images of people. The fix took months. Respect the culture, or build a bridge The temptation for founders and product builders is always to focus on the raw technology: the compute power, the model architecture, the sheer wizardry of what a tool can do. But history rewards the technology that integrates seamlessly into how humans already behave. If you are building something new, you have only two choices: Fit into existing culture and…

articles.title: The Digital Euro: Solving Problems You Didn’t Have, With Rules You Don’t Write
articles.content: Be honest. Do you actually need a digital euro because payments weren’t convenient enough already? I pay for everything with my phone. Instantly. Even when I’m abroad. To be fair, I’m still glad we actually get to live in the 21st century. But a digital euro? And no, it’s not because they want to ban cash. Cash is already quietly fading out of daily use in Europe. It’s certainly not because someone at a central bank suddenly developed a burning passion for transparency and democratisation. So let’s look at what’s actually being built, who gets to set the rules, and most importantly, why it’s being built at all. A pilot is not a public launch (It’s just the rehearsal where nobody gets to leave) According to ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone’s speech on 5 November 2026, they plan a 12-month pilot in the second half of 2027. It will involve 36 payment service providers, including Deutsche Bank, UniCredit, Revolut, Stripe, and Adyen. Testing will cover ordinary situations: purchases, transfers, and refunds. Harmless on paper. For now. Full speech – ECB Digital euro pilot page 2029 is more of a wish than a deadline According to the ECB, the target for a possible first issuance is 2029, but only if the necessary legislation is adopted by the end of 2026. Only then would the Governing Council decide whether to issue it at all. Preparing a system and approving its use are two separate decisions. News headlines tend to treat them as the same thing. ECB on the timeline These aren’t “your” deposits It might come as a shock, but the balance you see in your banking app isn’t actually your money. It’s a promise from your local bank that they’ll repay it one day. A digital euro would move that promise even further away, all the way behind the walls of the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt. Apart from that minor detail, your brand-new digital euro would be almost identical to what you already use. It would still be worth one euro. It would still appear on your screen as if you owned it. And it would still not be immune to money printing, inflation, or devaluation. There is a catch. Under the proposed design it wouldn’t even pay the princely 0.05% interest some accounts currently offer. And there would be a limit on how much you could hold. Roughly €3,000 was one of the options analysed, not a final rule. Europe doesn’t want to depend on Visa and Mastercard Now, to be fair, there is one legitimate point in favor of the digital euro. For card payments, Europe still depends heavily on non-European companies, in practice, mainly Visa and Mastercard. A shared European payments infrastructure makes sense as a political and economic objective. The real test is whether regular people actually get enough out of the digital euro to bother switching. Good luck convincing 450 million people to just switch up their daily habits. Especially when the new system arrives with holding limits, no interest, and a few extra questions about why you’re using it. Offline like cash Now for the part everyone’s actually worried about: privacy. For offline payments, the intention is cash-like privacy, personal transaction details known only to the payer and the recipient. That does not mean the entire wallet would operate anonymously like cash. Anti-money-laundering checks would still apply when depositing, transferring or withdrawing funds. If losing privacy on offline transactions worries you, online payments are a whole different story. Naturally, the ECB promises to process data so it can’t be traced straight back to you. Your bank or payment provider would still have identification and other legal obligations. In other words, the ECB says it will not monitor everything you buy. Your local bank will. Programmable money? The ECB says the digital euro would not be programmable money. The issuer wouldn’t dictate where, when or on what you could spend it. That’s different from a conditional payment you choose to arrange yourself. So there’s no need for panic about…

articles.title: Educational Byte: What Is a Liquidity Pool in Crypto —and Why It Matters
articles.content: To understand this one, let’s first look at the "traditional" processes for exchanging money via digital platforms. We can commonly see two mechanisms: you exchange your currency directly against the exchange or provider’s own funds, or an order book is used. This order book records all buy and sell orders placed by users and provides liquidity based on that activity. The more orders in place, the more liquidity. Well, liquidity pools have come to replace these models in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols. A liquidity pool in crypto is a supply of tokens locked inside a smart contract on a DeFi protocol. It has the purpose of offering liquidity to other users for swaps, loans, or any financial activity on that specific protocol. The locked funds come from other users who, in exchange for providing this liquidity to the pool, receive rewards in the form of transaction fees and even governance tokens . This way, no powerful middlemen are required to safely access financial instruments. It’s the users themselves who provide liquidity in a decentralized environment. How Does a Liquidity Pool Work? Typically, a liquidity pool holds two tokens, such as GBYTE and USDC. Liquidity providers are the ones who deposit these token pairs—and they could be anyone with the available funds. Then, those funds help to create a big reserve that traders can use for their own operations, like swaps. The smart contract keeps track of those balances and applies the rules that govern each trade. Price adjustment comes from the reserves themselves. In a classic Automated Market Maker (AMM) model, a simple formula is used: X × Y = K, where X and Y represent the quantities of the two tokens and K is the constant. When someone swaps, let’s say, USDC for GBYTE, the pool receives one asset and releases the other, changing the balances and thus the price for the next trade. Depending on the available liquidity, a larger trade may create more price impact, which implies that the price could drop by a certain percentage for the next swap. For liquidity providers, the platform may give them LP tokens as proof of their share of the pool. These tokens can be used to track and redeem that share, including the depositor’s portion of trading fees earned by the pool. Their reward is directly proportional to their contribution to the pool. Some pools may be rewarded with additional incentives . For instance, in the Obyte-based DEX Oswap.io , all liquidity providers to a few selected pools receive 100 GBYTE every seven days, distributed in proportion to their contributed liquidity. That’s an additional incentive on top of fees. Why Does This Model Matter? A healthy financial environment needs liquidity, and liquidity doesn’t come out of nowhere. For trades and other operations to actually happen, funds must be available, and someone must put the funds there. In traditional finance, that someone is often a powerful middleman, like a bank. But cryptocurrencies weren’t created to rely on powerful middlemen; they were created to get rid of them. So, we have liquidity pools instead. By using this model, everyone can access liquidity without cumbersome requirements or censorship risks . Meanwhile, liquidity providers receive rewards for their contributions in what is, without a doubt, a type of investment that can yield a good and frequent passive return. Of course, the specific rules and the censorship resistance vary from network to network. Obyte uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structure without miners or “validators,” which increases its decentralization and drastically reduces the mere possibility of censorship or blocking. In Oswap.io, each pool has its own parameters and governance, but all are decentralized and open for everyone to participate. That’s the whole idea; that’s why liquidity pools matter: they offer a freedom we can’t enjoy in traditional financial products. Featured Vector Image by pikisuperstar / Magnific

articles.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Is a Wake-Up Call for Startup Founders
articles.content: Why Nvidia's board could remove its founder CEO, and how startup founders can use dual-class shares, board seats, and voting control to protect their companies The Unthinkable Happened on a Thursday I had to read the headline three times. This morning, November 12, 2026, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, CEO, and director, effective immediately . CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair , which tells you it had been a one-man show for 33 years. The board's word is "resigned." Most headlines went with "ousted." Days earlier, CBS had reported the board was preparing to remove him. You decide which word fits. Here's the short version. A New York Times report alleged multiple affairs, including one with a Singapore data-center executive whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, at a firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia hardware. Another alleged affair was with a senior executive who reported directly to him. Huang had already admitted infidelity in a memo to employees on November 9. Then came national-security questions, demands from lawmakers, and a stock that fell roughly 10%, wiping out hundreds of billions in market value. After that, the end came quickly. Set the morality aside for a minute, because the board didn't need to settle it. What I want founders to notice is the mechanics . Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in a Denny's in 1993. He bet the company on GPUs, then on CUDA, then on AI, and grew it into a company worth more than $4 trillion. He is about as close to a founder-god as Silicon Valley has. And he had no structural protection whatsoever. Nvidia has a single class of stock: one share, one vote. Its board was made up of independent directors plus Jensen, and it could remove the CEO with or without cause by simple majority. Mark Zuckerberg can't be fired. Larry Page couldn't be fired. Jensen Huang, the man who made the AI age possible, could be shown the door in a week. If that doesn't make every founder reading this check their charter, nothing will. Jensen Huang at Stanford, April 2026, seven months before the fall. Thirty-three years of vision, and a single class of stock. Why Founders Fall: A Short History of Losing Your Own Company Founders don't usually lose control in one dramatic boardroom scene. They lose it gradually, through a series of small and individually reasonable decisions. Act I: One share, one vote. For about sixty years the NYSE refused to list companies with dual-class shares. The idea was that voting power should track economic risk. Ford's 1956 IPO, where the family kept super-voting shares, was the famous exception. Media dynasties like the New York Times Company got a pass on the grounds of editorial independence. Act II: Google changes the rules. In 2004, Larry Page and Sergey Brin took Google public with Class B shares carrying 10 votes each . The public bought it anyway. Facebook, LinkedIn, Snap, and Alibaba all followed. Hong Kong held out, lost Alibaba's $25 billion IPO to New York, and changed its rules in 2018. By 2021–22, about 47% of U.S. tech IPOs were dual-class. Act III: the slow loss of your majority. This is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. According to Carta's 2025–26 data, founders typically hold: The median founding team's stake by funding stage (Carta, 2025–26). By Series C, the option pool owns more of your company than you do. ~56% after Seed ~36% after Series A (thanks, pre-money option pool) ~23% after Series B ~16% after Series C, which is less than the employee option pool Capital intensity makes it worse. If your company works with atoms (chips, robots, biotech), you burn two to three times the cash of a SaaS company and sell more of the company at every round. Jensen is the hardware founder's cautionary tale: decades of capital-hungry growth, and nothing left to vote with when it counted. The lesson: you don't lose control when the…

articles.title: Claude Merged 30,401 Changes in One Day. Git Couldn't Keep Up.
articles.content: An agent gets a task - fix a flaky test. Before it reads a single line of code, it needs a working copy of the repository. Under git, that meant waiting 7.1 minutes. Multiply that wait by tens of thousands of agents a day and you get the problem Anthropic described in its engineering post on 13 October 2026. The code wasn't the slow part any more. Claude could write the fix in seconds; the plumbing built for human engineers (source control, builds, CI) couldn't hand it the repo fast enough. So Anthropic threw out git for its main repository and built Scion. January: about 1,000 merges a day The numbers tell the story better than I can. In January 2026, Anthropic merged roughly 1,000 code changes a day. By May it was about 2,500. The team tried everything git offers to cope: shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred git mirrors. Each one bought time. None of them bought enough, because the main-branch history was close to 100 GB and the compressed working copy was over 25 GB. CI alone ran around 25 million checkouts a day. The mirrors eventually outgrew their disks. At that point you can split the monorepo (and lose speed) or rebuild source control. Anthropic picked the second option. 9 September: 30,401 merges By September, Anthropic was merging more than 30,000 changes a day. The peak was 30,401 on 9 September. That's a 12x jump in four months, and most of it came from Claude. That's the day git stopped being a tool and became a ceiling. What Scion actually is Scion looks more like Subversion than git, and Anthropic says so openly. Git assumes every client is a full copy of history that can work offline. Scion assumes the opposite: clients are always online, so the server does the heavy lifting. The stack has four layers: scn , the client that runs on a developer laptop or inside an agent's sandbox scion-daemon , one per machine, which shares cached objects across every job on that node scion-cache , regional caches that sit between the machines and the source of truth scion-server , the authoritative layer, backed by Google Spanner and cloud storage Anthropic reports a cache hit rate above 99% at every tier. Almost nothing travels all the way to the servers. The unit of history changes too. A git commit points to a full tree. A Scion changeset lists only the files that changed relative to its first parent, each with a content-addressed pointer to a compressed blob. The server works out trees, history and blame from those changesets when someone asks. Branches are discouraged, except for main and release branches. Creating a changeset never touches a branch; moving one is a single compare-and-swap on one Spanner row. That's why 30,000 merges a day don't trip over each other. How Claude ships a change on Scion, step by step Anthropic's post doesn't publish a single runbook, so this is the flow pieced together from what the team described. Follow one agent and one flaky test. Step 1: Get a worktree in seconds. Claude asks scn for a working copy. It doesn't clone anything. The client names the root tree it wants and fetches only the objects it's missing, usually from the local daemon. Checkouts are sparse or virtual: a file lands on disk only when Claude opens it. A new agent worktree went from 7.1 minutes to 5.1 seconds, an 84x speedup. Step 2: Ask the server questions instead of the disk. Where was this test last changed? Who touched this function? Under git, Claude would run git log or git blame over local history. Under Scion, history, blame and diffs are server queries exposed through an API. Many jobs never need a local repository at all; Anthropic says its automated bisect and revert pipelines wouldn't be practical at scale without this. Step 3: Edit, and let status stay cheap. Claude changes two files. The client watches the filesystem rather than rescanning the whole tree, so checking status for an agent fell from 4.3 seconds to under 0.2. Step 4: Commit straight to…

articles.title: C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute
articles.content: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup , who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies. The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay. Contracts dispute Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior. Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel . Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults. But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal ( P2900 ) that made it into C++26. “The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested , and could be more effectively implemented as a library. Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig , a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself. “The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post . The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adpot Rust . Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language . Sore losers Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers. “Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust." Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself. “The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.” Where to now? With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next…

articles.title: Microsoft struggles to get M365 services back online after widespread outage
articles.content: If you’re struggling to send or receive emails, you’re not alone. Microsoft has been unable to fully restore Microsoft 365 more than 13 hours after an Exchange Online failure took down Outlook and spread to Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and parts of the company’s security tooling, and it said overnight that its latest fixes were “not taking as expected.” The outage began at 16:17 UTC on Nov. 12, according to Microsoft’s service health dashboard . “Users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop (MAPI), Exchange ActiveSync (EAS), or REST-based connections, and email delivery may be delayed,” Microsoft wrote in the dashboard. Users in the Americas could not reach their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop Outlook, mobile clients, or the REST API. Within two hours, Microsoft said users in any region could be affected. It opened a wider incident covering Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot, Defender XDR, Intune, Power BI, and several Purview services. Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak. In its latest service-health updates for incident MO1550821 , Microsoft said it had observed a surge in calls from routing services to backend servers as it applied mitigation measures. The company said traffic rebalancing had contributed to the increased volume and that it was scaling virtual machines to add capacity and reduce the load. “As we’ve applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers,” Microsoft said in the update. It added: “We’re continuing to observe heightened volume due to traffic rebalancing actions that we have taken throughout this event.” Server failures behind the disruption Microsoft initially investigated elevated infrastructure load and the possibility that a recent change had contributed to the incident. It later said the problem was not being driven by an overall increase in traffic. “We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure,” the company said in its Exchange Online incident update . In a subsequent update, Microsoft identified a process responsible for establishing secure connections as a source of the problem. “Our investigation has found that a process on the affected servers responsible for establishing secure connections becomes overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests,” the company said. Microsoft said it was preparing a configuration change to address the behaviour and testing it on a subset of servers before wider deployment. It was also reverting a recent network configuration change that correlated with the start of the disruption, while restarting affected infrastructure and monitoring server stability. The recovery process has involved restricting some traffic and gradually reintroducing connections as Microsoft checks whether servers can remain stable under load. The company also reported that some servers became unresponsive again after traffic was restored, requiring further analysis and mitigation. Impact extends beyond email Microsoft’s incident notification said the impact varied by service and feature, depending in part on whether they relied on Exchange Online. The company said users might be unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes through Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop, Exchange ActiveSync, or REST-based connections, and that email delivery might be delayed. It said Teams’ core messaging and online meetings remained largely functional, but Exchange-dependent features such as calendar access and meeting scheduling could fail. Microsoft also said that direct access to files stored in SharePoint Online remained functional, while features dependent on Exchange Online could be affected. articles.title: Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
articles.content: The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report: "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales. "Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. This will tell us where galaxies are in space and time, across 10 billion years, and in all directions beyond our galactic plane," Pettorino said. "Galaxies cluster along filaments, surrounded by empty space, and form a network that we call the cosmic web. Euclid will reconstruct the cosmic web and how it has grown over time. This is important because the exact configuration of the cosmic web, how many clusters or voids are there, how fast it changed, depend on the properties of dark energy and dark matter," Pettorino said. [...] Previous Euclid data releases covered only a few days of observations. The newly released dataset includes more than a year of data and still spans only 14% of the total sky area Euclid is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years. This data release will be completed next year with the first results on dark energy and dark matter. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Microsoft's massive M365 outage stretches past 12 hours as its fixes keep failing
articles.content: In Australia, they’re calling it the “Microsoft long weekend” – an outage so pervasive it’s just about made Friday a write-off at organizations which rely on Redmond’s online services, especially Exchange Online. As The Register reported yesterday , the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services. The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional. The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.” In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service. It has also changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility that a cyberattack is the reason for the outage. As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.” Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order: We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online; We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected; We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability; We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances; We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery; Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected. Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon. “We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.” Hopefully, Australia and other countries in nearby time zones won’t be the only ones to get an unscheduled long weekend. ®

articles.title: Developer cleverly shrank 2,600 lines of C into a six-line script but still ending up losing sleep
articles.content: Working in tech support can be thankless when gormless colleagues leave you sleepless. Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script. He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP). "Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote. This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases. "In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the struct proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code." Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe. "It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained. The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night. After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague. But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot. So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions. How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? If you have enough energy, click here to send your story with On Call so we can share it on a future Friday. ®

articles.title: New AI “copilot” helps engineers design better structures
articles.content: The use of algorithms to design structures has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas, and F1 racing cars. But the best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time: Users only see the final design after it’s complete, after which they often must start the design process all over again to make changes. That process also makes it harder to trust that the final designs are structurally sound. MIT researchers are making algorithmic designs more collaborative with a system that acts like an AI copilot. As the algorithm is generating the structure, it presents regions to the human designer for feedback. In an open-access Communications Engineering paper describing the system, the researchers showed it led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads while adding only 15 seconds to the total design time compared to all-algorithmic approaches. The researchers believe the approach, which uses a design technique known as topology optimization, could make algorithmic design more accessible and manufacturable for a broader class of design engineers. “Right now, the human doesn’t have any agency or control over the design process as it’s playing out,” explains lead author Dat Ha PhD ’26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student who is now a structural designer at LeMessurier. “For these really complex designs, we wanted to also tap into our brain, which is the most complex machine there is, to solve these design problems in a way that’s more practical to industry.” Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering. Bringing a human in the loop Topology optimization is one of the most advanced and promising algorithmic design techniques. It uses formal optimization techniques to iteratively fill in the space given for a design in a way that maximally achieves the stated goals. For most applications, the process requires a lot of computation and time. When it’s finally done, the designs can be impractical to build or have other issues the engineer didn’t consider. For instance, some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world. “Engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give you very weird-looking or unexpected designs,” Ha says. “On paper, topology optimization is really powerful and can achieve great, high-performing designs, but its black box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry.” Topology optimization has gotten traction in the automotive and aerospace industries, but it’s been used less to design buildings or bridges, partly because design engineers need to know they can trust the output. “A big limiting factor has been that the design engineer has very little influence over how the design evolves and therefore can’t control undesirable features,” Carstensen explains. “The lack of control and lack of ownership also inhibits its use.” To address those problems, the researchers made topology optimization more collaborative in an approach that Carstensen compares to having a design copilot. Prior attempts at adding human judgment slowed things down dramatically. The researchers’ new system uses machine learning to quickly identify the most likely regions of an algorithmic design that a human would want to change. To train the machine-learning model, the researchers created a synthetic dataset of probable human feedback to thousands of designs that critiqued things like aesthetics, performance criteria, and manufacturability. “We thought if we could create a record of where humans have made changes to these…

articles.title: Helping robots fit into the human workplace
articles.content: Despite fears about robots replacing humans at work, there are still plenty of things humans can do far better than machines. That’s fine with Robust AI, a startup building robots designed to complement what humans do best. The company’s mobile robot, named Carter, resembles a utility cart on wheels and is designed to fit seamlessly alongside humans in fast-changing warehouse and factory environments. Carter features a force-sensitive handlebar for easy guidance, an AI-powered vision system, and holonomic wheels for instant movement in any direction. As a result, humans can cut Carter off, push and pull it in any direction with one hand, and direct it with gestures or the onboard touch screen. The company’s robots are currently deployed in logistics warehouses and on factory floors, where they help humans while picking or stocking shelves and moving items across facilities autonomously. “In these environments, what really determines success is how the overall system performs,” explains Anthony Jules ’92, SM ’92, who co-founded the company with MIT Professor Emeritus Rodney Brooks. “The robot does some of the work, the people do some of the work, and the backend systems do some of the work. It’s that combination that determines how well your system performs. We believe it’s really important that people have an appropriate level of agency and input so that they’re always moving the system forward.” Collaborative robots Brooks was a faculty member at MIT from 1984 until 2010 and served as the director of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) from 1997 until 2007. While at MIT, he co-founded iRobot, which invented the popular Roomba vacuum and went public in 2005. Later, he co-founded the company Rethink Robotics, which also designed collaborative robots. Jules met Brooks as a graduate student at CSAIL in the 1990s. The two never worked together, but their labs were on the same floor. The pair kept in touch after Jules graduated and co-founded the company Sapient, which went public before being acquired by Publicis in 2015. In 2019, Brooks bumped into Jules at a robotics conference. He told Jules he was thinking of starting a robotics software company, which he compared to a video game engine for training robots. Robust AI was founded later that year. The Covid-19 pandemic caused the founders to shift to creating robots that could autonomously disinfect surfaces, but when it was discovered that Covid-19 was not transmitted via surfaces, they had to pivot again. “That forced us to decide how to use this technology we had been building, which was really about helping robots understand the world more fully,” Jules recalls. “Long story short, I said to Rodney, ‘I have an idea. You’re going to love it and you’re going to hate it. You’re going to love it because it’s solving problems for customers that we’ve been hearing about, and you’re going to hate it because we have to build hardware.” The founders had been interviewing potential customers for years through Robust AI’s early pivots. They finally decided on logistics and manufacturing as the industries to target early on. “When people think about automation in factories, they think about pictures of the 5 percent that are fully automated with $50 to $200 million dollar systems,” says Jules, who now serves as Robust AI’s chief innovation officer. “They don’t think about the vast majority of factories that aren’t automated at all. These factories don’t even have a conveyor belt. They are not going to tear everything out and replace it with a $200 million system.” Robust AI’s robots can be phased into operations as needed and offer several workflows for customers. In one workflow, the robot can guide human workers to specific spaces to retrieve items. In another it can follow humans to important spots for loading. The primary workflows involve Carter robots moving things from one place to another, often in large warehouses or factories, where they say…

articles.title: Singapore says US authorities, and Supermicro, hardly helped investigation of Jensen Huang’s Chinese friend
articles.content: The government of Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs has revealed it investigated Alice Huang, the woman who is an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and a possible entanglement with troubled server-maker Supermicro. US authorities provided only “limited assistance” in the matter, despite Singapore asking for help. The Ministry outlined its activities in a statement published late on Thursday, Singapore time. The document reveals that Singapore’s Police Force (SPF) and Customs agency commenced an investigation into Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, in February 2025. “The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences,” the Ministry wrote, adding that the exec “was not investigated for espionage.” Singaporean authorities wanted to know if servers bought by local companies, but exported to Malaysia without ever touching Singaporean soil, might have ended up in a third country. It is not unusual for Singapore-based companies to acquire goods that never reach the island, because it promotes itself as the ideal spot from which to run an operation that trades across Asia. Singapore does so because it is tiny – the whole nation is the same size as the five boroughs of New York City. That small size means Singapore restricts the number of datacenters that can operate on its soil. Those limits are a big reason why Malaysia’s Johor region, which is under 20kms from the border with Singapore and a joint special economic zone, has become a major datacenter province. Singapore needs deals like that to thrive but works hard to ensure its hospitality is not abused. Which is why it felt Megaspeed’s activities worthy of investigation. US authorities were interested too. On 24 June 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security, which regulates sensitive goods subject to export controls, visited Megaspeed in Singapore to check the hardware it bought arrived at its intended destination. Ms. Huang attended that event and later met the SPF for an interview. That meeting ended with the SPF impounding her passport, so it could keep her in Singapore while the investigation continued. As the matter progressed, the SPF suspected perennially troubled server-maker Supermicro had a role in this situation. Readers may recall that the US Department of Justice indicted two Supermicro execs for conspiring to ship servers to China in contravention of US law. Supermicro investigated the matter and parted ways with three staff who acted improperly. The company has denied ever selling to Megaspeed. Singaporean authorities say they received only “limited cooperation” from Supermicro, so in July 2025 the office of the nation’s Attorney General asked US authorities for help. “Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation,” the statement reveals. “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company.” In February 2026, the SPF “concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.” But the police did decide that Ms. Huang provided inaccurate information “to downplay her role in Megaspeed.” “She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country.” The police returned her passport and Ms. Huang left Singapore on the same day. The Singaporean statement shows the island nation wants the world to know it does not facilitate sanction-busting activity and takes even the hint of it seriously. That matters to Nvidia, too, because Singaporean buyers sometimes account for over 20 percent of its quarterly revenue and may continue to do so. Whoever replaces Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO will surely face many…
